outputs.L1: We report a novel effect of surfactants on droplet contact-line pinning: lysozyme promotes pinning, whereas lauryl sulfate inhibits it. We attribute this disparity to differences in wetting behavior: a protein-laden droplet wets a “clean” surface, while a surfactant-laden droplet wets an auto-precursored surface.
outputs.L2: We describe a newly observed role of surfactants in anchoring a droplet’s contact line: lysozyme enhances this pinning, whereas lauryl sulfate reduces it. We attribute this contrast to differences in wetting behavior, proposing that a lysozyme-containing drop spreads over a clean surface, while a lauryl-sulfate-containing drop spreads over a surface already modified by an auto-precursor film.
outputs.L3:
Surfactants can significantly influence the pinning behavior of a droplet’s contact line. The contact line, where the liquid, solid, and surrounding air meet, may either remain fixed in place during evaporation or motion, or it may recede across the surface. This behavior is strongly affected by the chemical nature of the molecules present in the droplet.

In the case of lysozyme, a protein surfactant, the droplet contact line is promoted to pin. This means that the edge of the drop tends to remain fixed on the substrate rather than moving freely. Lysozyme-laden drops therefore show stronger contact-line anchoring, which can affect evaporation patterns, droplet shape, and deposited residues.

By contrast, lauryl sulfate inhibits pinning of the drop contact line. Drops containing lauryl sulfate are more likely to depin and spread or recede, indicating a weaker resistance to contact-line motion. This difference shows that not all surface-active molecules have the same effect on droplet dynamics.

The contrasting pinning behavior can be explained by differences in wetting behavior. Protein-laden drops, such as those containing lysozyme, tend to wet a clean solid surface directly. This direct interaction between the protein-containing liquid and the substrate can enhance adhesion at the contact line and promote pinning. In contrast, surfactant-laden drops containing lauryl sulfate wet an auto-precursored surface. In this case, surfactant molecules can spread ahead of the visible droplet edge, forming a thin precursor film on the substrate. The drop then effectively advances or recedes over a surface that has already been modified by the surfactant, reducing resistance to motion and inhibiting contact-line pinning.

Thus, the different effects of lysozyme and lauryl sulfate on contact-line pinning arise from the distinct ways in which protein- and surfactant-containing drops interact with the substrate. Lysozyme enhances pinning by promoting wetting of a clean surface, whereas lauryl sulfate suppresses pinning by creating or wetting an auto-precursored surface that facilitates contact-line motion.
outputs.L4:
The text investigates the role of surfactants in controlling droplet contact-line pinning, with particular attention to how different types of surface-active molecules can produce opposite wetting behaviors. Contact-line pinning refers to the tendency of the edge of a liquid drop to remain fixed in place as the droplet spreads, evaporates, or changes shape. This phenomenon is important because it influences the final footprint of a drop, the internal flow patterns that develop during evaporation, and the deposition patterns left behind on a surface.

To explore this effect, the discussion compares two representative additives: lysozyme, a protein, and lauryl sulfate, a low-molecular-weight surfactant. Although both substances are surface active, they interact with the liquid–air, liquid–solid, and solid–air interfaces in different ways. Lysozyme-laden droplets show a stronger tendency for the contact line to become pinned. In this case, the protein appears to enhance the ability of the droplet edge to remain anchored to the substrate. This behavior is consistent with a situation in which the drop wets a relatively clean solid surface, allowing the contact line to interact directly with surface heterogeneities or adsorbed protein structures that can resist motion.

By contrast, droplets containing lauryl sulfate exhibit reduced contact-line pinning. Instead of remaining fixed, the contact line is more mobile, indicating that this surfactant inhibits the mechanisms that normally hold the droplet edge in place. The text interprets this difference in terms of the wetting conditions created ahead of the visible contact line. Lauryl sulfate can generate or stabilize an “auto-precursor” film, a very thin layer of liquid or surfactant-rich material that spreads in advance of the macroscopic drop. As a result, the apparent contact line no longer advances over a clean dry surface, but over a surface that has already been modified or prewetted by this precursor layer. This reduces resistance to motion and weakens pinning.

The comparison between lysozyme and lauryl sulfate therefore shows that surfactants cannot be treated as having a single universal effect on contact-line dynamics. Their influence depends on their molecular nature, adsorption behavior, and ability to alter the wetting state of the substrate. Protein-containing drops tend to wet clean surfaces and promote pinning, whereas lauryl-sulfate-containing drops tend to wet auto-precursored surfaces and suppress pinning. The central conclusion is that the presence or absence of contact-line pinning is governed not only by surface roughness or evaporation dynamics, but also by the microscopic wetting environment established by the dissolved surface-active species.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract-style summary of a study finding that lysozyme enhances contact line pinning in drying droplets while lauryl sulfate suppresses it, explaining the mechanism through different wetting conditions.
counterfactuals.output: This study examines how solutes with contrasting interfacial behaviors influence contact line dynamics in drying droplets. Lysozyme-containing droplets exhibit enhanced contact line pinning, whereas droplets with lauryl sulfate show suppressed pinning and easier contact line recession. The difference arises from their distinct wetting conditions and interfacial effects: lysozyme promotes stronger droplet–substrate adhesion and stabilizes the pinned contact line, likely through adsorption or deposition near the contact line, while lauryl sulfate lowers surface tension and improves wetting mobility, reducing the resistance to depinning. These results demonstrate that solute-specific interfacial interactions can regulate evaporation patterns by controlling whether the contact line remains pinned or retracts during drying.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main conclusion of a paper about surfactant effects on droplet contact line pinning, contrasting protein lysozyme and lauryl sulfate and mentioning clean versus auto-precursored surfaces.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper’s main conclusion is that surfactants affect droplet contact-line pinning mainly through their adsorption/deposition at the solid surface and near the contact line, not simply through lowering the liquid–air surface tension.

In the comparison studied:

- **Lysozyme**, a protein, tends to adsorb/accumulate irreversibly and form a more robust deposit at the contact line, so it **enhances pinning** and can leave a strongly anchored “ring” during evaporation or recession.
- **Lauryl sulfate** behaves more like a mobile small-molecule surfactant: it can spread or adsorb ahead of the visible contact line, creating an **auto-precursor film** that modifies the substrate before the drop edge arrives. This can reduce or change pinning relative to a clean surface.

Thus, the same droplet can behave differently on a **clean surface** versus an **auto-precursored surface** already coated by surfactant from the drop itself. The study emphasizes that contact-line motion depends on the evolving surfactant-conditioned substrate, and that proteins such as lysozyme and surfactants such as lauryl sulfate produce qualitatively different pinning behavior.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

Lysozyme enhances contact line pinning, whereas lauryl sulfate suppresses pinning, indicating that surfactant identity can oppositely regulate wetting hysteresis and interfacial force balance.

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal research-paper language, state the key finding that lysozyme and lauryl sulfate have opposite effects on contact line pinning and explain this using differences in wetting behavior.
counterfactuals.output: Lysozyme and lauryl sulfate exert opposing influences on contact-line pinning: lysozyme enhances or stabilizes pinning of the receding contact line, whereas lauryl sulfate promotes depinning and contact-line mobility. This contrast can be attributed to their distinct effects on wetting behavior. Lysozyme tends to increase surface heterogeneity or adsorption-mediated adhesion at the solid–liquid interface, thereby increasing resistance to contact-line motion and sustaining a pinned state. In contrast, lauryl sulfate, as an anionic surfactant, reduces interfacial tension and improves wetting/spreading, which lowers the energetic barrier for contact-line displacement and facilitates depinning. Thus, the observed difference in pinning behavior reflects the different ways in which the protein and surfactant modify interfacial interactions and the dynamic wetting properties of the substrate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a brief conclusion for a physics paper on surfactant-laden drops: lysozyme pins the contact line, lauryl sulfate prevents pinning, due to protein drops wetting clean surfaces and surfactant drops wetting auto-precursored surfaces.
counterfactuals.output: In conclusion, the contrasting evaporation and spreading dynamics of lysozyme- and lauryl-sulfate-laden drops arise from their distinct interactions with the substrate. Lysozyme promotes contact-line pinning because protein-containing drops wet an initially clean solid surface, leading to strong adhesion at the three-phase line. In contrast, lauryl sulfate suppresses pinning by generating an auto-precursor film ahead of the macroscopic drop, so that the advancing and receding contact lines move over a surfactant-prewetted surface. These results highlight that contact-line mobility in surfactant-laden drops is governed not only by surface-tension reduction, but also by whether the drop encounters a clean or self-conditioned substrate.
